S&P 500

ES=F close · close 7,237.25

-2 stretched-down

ES=F closed 7237.25 on 25 November (from 7200.00, +0.52%) after one of the widest intraday round trips in this ledger's short record: the contract printed a labelled hourly swing low of 6982.50 at 09:00 ET, 3.02% below Tuesday's close, and finished 3.65% above that low. The cash index did the same thing in smaller type, falling as much as 3.2% to 6,970.11 before closing down just 0.25% (-18.31) at 7,182.78, while the Dow erased an intraday loss of more than 1,100 points - a low of 48,913.74 - to close up 0.33% (+164.25) at 50,182.95, its second straight close above 50,000, and the Nasdaq Composite recovered from -4.6% to -0.62% (-147.74) at 23,585.80 (CappNotes Closing Look and theweekendspread, 25 November). The morning was driven by two things on the news log: October PCE at 8:30 ET, where core accelerated to 3.3% year-on-year against a 3.2% consensus and 3.1% prior with headline at 3.8%, the highest annual reading in three years, alongside a Q3 GDP second estimate revised up to a 4.3% annualised rate from 3.4% against a consensus near 3.5%; and a proposed Section 301 tariff schedule covering 14 trading partners at up to 20% on China and 15% on the EU and Japan, stacking above 40% in some categories, which an official said would take effect in January at the earliest after hearings and a comment period (news log entries 1, 2 and 4, 25 November). Asia had already led the unwind rather than followed it: the Kospi fell 6.16% to 4,697.51, its weakest close since 13 January, triggering a sell-side sidecar on the Korea Exchange, the Taiex fell 4.80%, and the Nikkei 2.78% to 57,011.62 with SoftBank -14.83% to a 52-week low. What turned the US tape was specific and reported: technology pared losses late in the day after reports that US officials told congressional staffers there was no evidence that a Chinese technology executive linked to the Jensen Huang affair had been directed by Chinese intelligence to spy on Huang (gsmglobalnews market close, 25 November). Underneath the index the session was overwhelmingly positive: 370 advancers to 128 decliners with roughly three quarters of the S&P 500's members higher, nine of eleven sectors up - Materials +2.07%, Real Estate +0.92%, Communication Services +0.89%, Industrials +0.83%, Energy +0.74%, Financials +0.71% - against only Consumer Discretionary -0.20%, Health Care -0.56% and Technology -0.83%, with equal-weight RSP +0.83%, the S&P MidCap 400 +1.23% and the SmallCap 600 +0.81%. The VIX rose 7.32% to 28.29 having topped 30 in the morning. Rates went the other way from the inflation print: the 10-year fell 6bp to 4.85%, the 30-year 6bp to 5.24% and the 2-year 2bp to 4.61%, flattening 2s10s to about 24bp, through a $44 billion 7-year auction that cleared at a 4.708% high yield with a 1bp tail and a 2.43x bid-to-cover. A 25bp hike on 9 December is priced at 97.8% on CME FedWatch, 94% on Polymarket and 93% on Kalshi.written Thu Nov 26, 9:52 AM ET · data through Wed Nov 25 close

why this stretch score
  • Two components fire for a score of -2 (stretched-down), unchanged in label from 24 November but shallower underneath. extension50 is -1: ES=F at 7237.25 is 5.30% under its 50-day (7642.04) for a z50 of -2.97 at a VIX of 28.29, where it was -3.53 last session, and still well short of the -4 that extension50 needs for -2. extension200 stays dormant at a z200 of -1.10 against a -6 threshold; the close is 1.96% below the 200-day (7381.71).
  • The second component is the crowd input at -1, carried from 24 November on sourcing that is now partly dated on S itself. It is not a judgment about how crowded the market feels: it records that named sources themselves give percentile and multi-year extremes for US equity positioning. Goldman Sachs told clients on 25 November that its Sentiment and Positioning Indicator had fallen to the 36th percentile, its lowest reading since April 2025. The 23-24 November prime-brokerage material this ledger already recorded adds fundamental long/short net leverage of 42.3% at the 1st or 5th percentile of the past year depending on the account, beta-adjusted net leverage of 48.2% described as a five-year low, and the largest weekly single-stock shorting flow since June 2022. See nullInputs for the exact sourcing and the disagreement between accounts. At -1 rather than -2 the value stays deliberately conservative for figures reached through secondary reporting, and it is left unchanged even though Wednesday's 3.65% intraday recovery off the low plausibly released some of that positioning - no dated post-session positioning figure exists to say how much.
  • RSI 40.71, up from 39.32, is well clear of the -1 oscillator threshold of 30, and the close sits 8.09% below the 252-session closing high (7874.00) and 13.29% above the low (6388.25), so the range component is dormant at both ends. All three equity cells resolve to flat, which the overlay leaves untouched: a flat cell is not a directional continuation bet.
written Thu Nov 26, 9:52 AM ET · data through Wed Nov 25 close
what's been moving this (4)
  • Macro · High impact · Wed Nov 25, Pre-marketOctober PCE, the last major inflation print before the Dec 8-9 FOMC, came in hot. Headline PCE rose to 3.8% y/y, the highest annual reading since 2023, and core PCE accelerated to 3.3% y/y, above the 3.2% consensus and up from 3.1% in September. Consumer spending rose 0.3% m/m after an upwardly revised 0.6% in September. Traders now price a ~98% chance of a 25bp December rate HIKE from the current 3.75%-4.00% range, with another increase expected in January; Governor Waller has signaled he could back 50bp.
  • Policy · High impact · Wed Nov 25, Pre-marketThe Trump administration proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on China, the EU and 12 other major trading partners, following an eight-month USTR investigation into excess manufacturing capacity and industrial subsidies. The duties would stack on existing tariffs, pushing total rates above 40% in some categories, with China expected to face the higher end. Final rates are not set: the proposal goes through hearings and a public comment period and an official said it would likely take effect in January at the earliest. The existing US-China trade truce expires January 10.
  • Market · High impact · Wed Nov 25, Pre-marketMonday's Jensen Huang-return melt-up has fully reversed into a global chip rout. Asia closed sharply lower: the Kospi plunged 6.16% to its weakest close since Jan 13, triggering a sell-side sidecar on the Korea Exchange, while SoftBank sank about 14.8% to a 52-week low and dragged the Nikkei down 2.8%. Nvidia, which fell 5.9% on Tuesday, dropped another 5-6% premarket, with AMD, Intel, Micron and Dell all down more. Investors are again questioning the payoff on AI infrastructure spending and circular financing, with Anthropic trading below its $83 IPO price.
  • Macro · Medium impact · Wed Nov 25, Pre-marketThe BEA's second estimate put Q3 real GDP growth at a 4.3% annualized rate, a large upward revision from the 3.4% advance estimate and above the ~3.5% consensus, versus 2.2% in Q2. Quarterly core PCE was 2.5%, in line, and the GDP price index came in at 1.8%, below the 2.3% consensus. The release landed alongside October PCE at 8:30 AM ET, reinforcing the picture John Williams described on Tuesday: a strong economy with inflation still running too hot.
since the board (3) · news after Wed Nov 25 - not in these calls
  • Policy · High impact · Thu Nov 26, Pre-marketThe detail of Wednesday's tariff proposal landed far softer than the headline. Reuters reports the new duties on 14 trading partners will NOT stack on top of the tariffs imposed in July, are unlikely to take effect until February or March (versus the January timeline floated Wednesday), and leave several key import categories exempt, including tech goods; Irish pharmaceutical exports were also spared. China still faces the highest proposed rate at 20%. The measures stem from a Section 301 investigation launched after the Supreme Court struck down the earlier sweeping tariffs, and still face hearings and a comment period.
  • Market · High impact · Thu Nov 26, Pre-marketYesterday's global chip rout reversed hard overnight with Wall Street closed. Japan's Nikkei 225 closed +0.9% at 57,499.16 with SoftBank +7.3% and Kioxia +12.6%, recovering part of Wednesday's 14.8% and 14.2% slides; Taiwan's Taiex jumped 2.5%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng +1.2%, and Korea's Kospi added 0.3% after Wednesday's 6.2% sidecar-triggering collapse, while the Shanghai Composite was flat. Europe followed in size: DAX +1.9%, CAC 40 +1.8%, FTSE 100 +1.6%, with the broad European tape up about 1.6% and the MSCI global index +0.4%.
  • Geopolitics · High impact · Thu Nov 26, Pre-marketOil extended a three-day rally after the Houthis claimed a strike on Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom's largest at 550,000 b/d. Satellite imagery showed a large black smoke plume and CNN reported loadings at the terminal were suspended; the Saudi-led coalition confirmed destroying four drones over Ras Tanura but has not confirmed the refinery itself was hit. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed two tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz without Tehran's permission were struck by sea mines north of Khasab - an Iranian claim with no independent confirmation. Hormuz traffic remains disrupted ahead of the OPEC+ meeting on Nov 29.

The Beige Book at 2pm was the session's one soft data point: eight of twelve districts reported slight-to-moderate growth, down from nine in October, with four reporting no change, consumer spending roughly flat, auto sales softening and residential real estate weakening - against employment rising modestly, wage growth picking up in Philadelphia, Minneapolis and Dallas, and input costs from energy, transportation and tariffs rising faster than firms could pass on (Federal Reserve, 25 November). So the note was bid on growth fear and haven demand, not on any easing in the policy path: a 25bp hike on 9 December is priced at 97.8% on CME FedWatch, 94% on Polymarket and 93% on Kalshi, Governor Waller has said he could back 50bp, and Vice Chair Jefferson, speaking at UC San Diego, named the inflation path as the key guide while declining to signal the timing or size of a December move. Long-term Treasury ETFs took in $2.40 billion on the session, the second-largest category inflow behind US large-cap blend's $6.57 billion. Bonds' measured 21-session correlation to the 10-year is -0.964, the strongest single driver relationship in this document, so this asset is very nearly the 10-year's mirror; its correlation to oil is only -0.134, which matters because Brent rose 3.51% to $94.61 on the session.written Thu Nov 26, 9:52 AM ET · data through Wed Nov 25 close

Silver did the same thing harder - a low of $38.090, described as its lowest in more than a year, against a high of $41.590, closing near $41.120, up 0.78%. Vendors disagree on gold's level by about $50 and the disagreement is recorded in nullInputs rather than resolved: CappNotes has $3,534.70, -0.71%; Kitco about $3,576.30, +0.60%; goldprice.org 3580.16; Rio Times US$3,548; this ledger's own GC=F at 3586.20, which runs above spot on cost of carry in any case. The trigger was October PCE at 8:30 ET - core 3.3% year-on-year against a 3.2% consensus, headline 3.8%, the highest annual reading in three years - with a 25bp December hike priced at 97.8% on CME FedWatch and Governor Waller open to 50bp, which is the straightforward headwind for a non-yielding asset. What turned it was the same thing that turned equities: the 10-year fell 6bp to 4.85% and the 30-year 6bp to 5.24% in a haven bid, and North American equities reversed, which Kitco names explicitly as what helped stabilise the metals. Two things cut against the rebound. Gold-backed ETFs lost about $2.2 billion in the week to 20 November, their heaviest weekly exit since June, with holdings down 20.7 tonnes to 4,247.3 tonnes and North America accounting for 11.8 of those tonnes and Europe 6.4, and net withdrawals in three of the five weeks through 24 November for a cumulative drawdown near 30 tonnes (World Gold Council data via Reuters-sourced coverage). And oil, this asset's dominant measured driver at a 21-session correlation of -0.569, rose hard: Brent +3.51% to $94.61 after Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, and on Riyadh's financial district - an unverified claim - with Iran's navy saying two tankers were set ablaze the same day, and WTI +1.99% to $83.68. On the measured sign that is a headwind; on the mechanism a live Middle East supply threat is normally a gold tailwind, and the two readings are left in conflict in the Cross-asset votes rather than reconciled. Against the ETF selling, central banks bought 321 tonnes in the July-September quarter, the heaviest official-sector pace since late 2024, which the Council itself cautions is too erratic to guarantee a floor.written Thu Nov 26, 9:52 AM ET · data through Wed Nov 25 close

NQ=F close · close 26,278.25

-3 extreme-down

NQ=F closed 26278.25 on 25 November, up 0.30% from 26198.50, after printing a labelled hourly swing low of 25027.50 at 09:00 ET and closing 5.00% above it. The cash Nasdaq-100 fell 0.64% to 26,046.90, and at its low it stood exactly 20% below its October closing peak - touching bear-market territory on the session and closing out of it (gsmglobalnews market close, 25 November). The Nasdaq Composite recovered from -4.6% intraday to -0.62% at 23,585.80. This was the full reversal of Monday's Jensen Huang-return melt-up and it was led from Asia, not followed there: the Kospi fell 6.16% to 4,697.51, its weakest close since 13 January, triggering a sell-side sidecar on the Korea Exchange, with SK Hynix -10.32% and Samsung Electronics -9.87%; the Taiex fell 4.80% to 38,195.43 with MediaTek about -10%; the Nikkei 2.78% to 57,011.62 with SoftBank -14.83% to a 52-week low, Kioxia -14.18% and Advantest -12.94% (news log entry 3 and CappNotes, 25 November). In the US the damage was deep intraday and largely repaired by the close: Nvidia traded down more than 9% and closed -3.91% at $149.30, down about 27% in November, on a day range of $141.17 to $150.37, with S&P Global placing its AA rating on CreditWatch Negative; Broadcom fell more than 6% intraday to close -0.07%; Microsoft slid more than 3% to close -1.2%; Oracle closed -5.13% at $103.88 after a 52-week intraday low of $99.34; Micron -4.53%, Lam Research -5.68%, Amazon -3.12%, Alphabet -2.13%. SOXX finished -0.50% and SMH -1.01%, both far off their lows. Against that, Meta rose 3.40%, Salesforce 2.0%, Workday 0.68%, and Dell closed +0.60% after reporting record revenue of $54.94 billion and an AI backlog of $132.3 billion - a strong print the market paid almost nothing for. Technology was the weakest S&P 500 sector at -0.83% on a day nine of eleven sectors rose and roughly three quarters of the index's members were higher, so this index's own internals were the market's worst. The macro leg was October PCE - core 3.3% year-on-year against 3.2% expected, headline 3.8%, a three-year high - plus a Q3 GDP second estimate of 4.3% annualised and a proposed Section 301 tariff schedule on 14 trading partners at up to 20% on China and 15% on the EU and Japan. The recovery catalyst was reported: technology pared losses late after reports that US officials told congressional staffers there was no evidence that a Chinese technology executive linked to the Huang affair had been directed by Chinese intelligence to spy on him. Technology ETFs took in $2.30 billion on the session even as disruptive-tech funds lost $1.35 billion and thematic multi-sector funds $1.54 billion. This asset's dominant measured driver is the 10-year at a 21-session correlation of +0.429, and the 10-year fell 6bp to 4.85% - on the measured sign a headwind, and the index rose anyway, a conflict the Rates votes record rather than resolve.written Thu Nov 26, 9:52 AM ET · data through Wed Nov 25 close

what's been moving this (3)
  • Macro · High impact · Wed Nov 25, Pre-marketOctober PCE, the last major inflation print before the Dec 8-9 FOMC, came in hot. Headline PCE rose to 3.8% y/y, the highest annual reading since 2023, and core PCE accelerated to 3.3% y/y, above the 3.2% consensus and up from 3.1% in September. Consumer spending rose 0.3% m/m after an upwardly revised 0.6% in September. Traders now price a ~98% chance of a 25bp December rate HIKE from the current 3.75%-4.00% range, with another increase expected in January; Governor Waller has signaled he could back 50bp.
  • Policy · High impact · Wed Nov 25, Pre-marketThe Trump administration proposed new tariffs of up to 20% on China, the EU and 12 other major trading partners, following an eight-month USTR investigation into excess manufacturing capacity and industrial subsidies. The duties would stack on existing tariffs, pushing total rates above 40% in some categories, with China expected to face the higher end. Final rates are not set: the proposal goes through hearings and a public comment period and an official said it would likely take effect in January at the earliest. The existing US-China trade truce expires January 10.
  • Market · High impact · Wed Nov 25, Pre-marketMonday's Jensen Huang-return melt-up has fully reversed into a global chip rout. Asia closed sharply lower: the Kospi plunged 6.16% to its weakest close since Jan 13, triggering a sell-side sidecar on the Korea Exchange, while SoftBank sank about 14.8% to a 52-week low and dragged the Nikkei down 2.8%. Nvidia, which fell 5.9% on Tuesday, dropped another 5-6% premarket, with AMD, Intel, Micron and Dell all down more. Investors are again questioning the payoff on AI infrastructure spending and circular financing, with Anthropic trading below its $83 IPO price.
